terms.gloss: close by, a door or two away
terms.grammar: adverbial phrase: in with the ablative of proximum
evidence: Plaut. Cist. 752: Ubi ea est …? — Hīc in proximō.
Plaut. Mil. 134: in proximō hīc dēvertitur
terms.comment: What Plautus’s people say of someone a door or two away, and so the phrase for a shop or a house that is just around the corner, usually with hīc. We have found no set phrase with angulus for this in the authors we searched or in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. Where the corner itself matters, say it plainly: post angulum of what stands or hides there, angulum circumīre of going round it. Both are descriptions of ours; see the examples. Of a day or a season that is close, īnstāre: hiems īnstat.

terms.gloss: at a bend in the road, out of sight round it
evidence: Liv. 22.12.7: in aliquō flexū viae … occultus subsistēbat
Levi–Bini p. 65: flexus viae, the turning of a street
terms.comment: Livy’s phrase for Hannibal lying in wait where the road turns.

phrases.english: The bakery is just around the corner.
The car is round the corner.
The cat is hiding round the corner.

phrases.latin: Nōlī angulum circumīre; hīc mē exspectā.
phrases.english: Don’t go round the corner; wait for me here.

phrases.latin: Ubi ea est, quae gestitāvit? — Hīc in proximō.
phrases.english: Where is she, the girl who used to wear them? — Close by, next door.

phrases.latin: nam et vēnit et is in proximō hīc dēvertitur
phrases.english: for he has come, and he is staying right here next door

phrases.latin: modo repente in aliquō flexū viae, sī excipere dēgressum in aequum posset, occultus subsistēbat
phrases.english: now he would suddenly halt, hidden round some bend in the road, in the hope of catching him as he came down onto level ground
for by now winter too was just around the corner

sources: Lewis & Short: proximus · Lewis & Short: flexus
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 65, s.v. svolta.
